title: System Design: From Classical Internet Systems to AI Inference and Training Platforms
description: Classical system design from first principles, then the same discipline applied to AI inference platforms and AI training infrastructure.

parts.title: Foundations of System Design
parts.description: The request-path, storage, coordination, and reliability mechanisms every later case study and platform design assumes.

modules.title: The Request Path: DNS, Load Balancers, Reverse Proxies, CDNs, and Edge Networks
modules.description: How a request travels from a client's DNS lookup to an origin server, and back, through every hop that can add latency or fail.
modules.scope: In: DNS resolution and anycast, L4 vs L7 load balancing algorithms (round robin, least-connections, ip-hash, weighted), reverse proxy responsibilities, CDN/edge PoP topology and tiered caching, the arithmetic of latency budgets across hops. Out: application-level caching semantics (Module 2), service-mesh sidecars (Module 10). After this module Aman can read a load balancer or CDN config and predict which requests land where and why, and can build a hop-by-hop latency budget for any request path in this course.
topics: DNS resolution and anycast routing
L4 vs L7 load balancing
round robin, least-connections, ip-hash, weighted algorithms and their failure modes
reverse proxy responsibilities (TLS termination, routing, buffering)
CDN/edge PoP topology and points of presence
tiered caching between edge and origin (Cloudflare Tiered Cache pattern)
session affinity and its cost
latency-budget arithmetic across DNS + LB + proxy + CDN hops
Netflix Open Connect as a purpose-built CDN contrasted with a general CDN

modules.title: Caching at Every Layer: Placement, Coherence, and Invalidation
modules.description: Every layer from browser to database row caches something; the module is about what breaks when the cached copy and the source of truth disagree.
modules.scope: In: cache placement (client, CDN/edge, reverse proxy, application, database buffer/block cache), cache-aside vs read-through vs write-through vs write-back, TTL-based vs event-based invalidation, cache stampede and thundering herd, popularity-tail-aware caching. Out: LLM-platform prompt/prefix caching, which is a distinct billing-bearing mechanism covered in Module 28. Coverage note: caching-invalidation is a thin subtopic in the source map -- no single company has published a dedicated 'caching at every layer' architecture document, so this module is grounded in CDN-tier and database-block-cache primary sources plus DDIA's synthesis, and states explicitly where a writer should look for more (e.g. a dedicated Redis/Memcached engineering post) if deeper application-cache mechanics are needed.
topics: cache placement across the stack: browser, CDN/edge, reverse proxy, application, DB buffer/block cache
cache-aside vs read-through vs write-through vs write-back
TTL-based expiry vs explicit event-based invalidation
cache stampede / thundering herd and mitigations (locking, jittered TTLs, request coalescing)
Cache Reserve as a higher, longer-retention tier requiring revalidation on TTL expiry
popularity-tail-aware caching: Netflix's 10-20% memory-resident titles vs NVMe for the rest
Bigtable's 64KB in-memory SSTable block index as a database-layer cache
write-behind risk: data loss window on cache-node failure

modules.title: Replication and Partitioning: Making One Dataset Look Like Many Machines
modules.description: The two independent decisions -- how many copies of the data exist, and which machine owns which slice -- that every storage system must make before anything else.
modules.scope: In: leader-follower and quorum replication, lease-based mutation ordering (GFS), consistent hashing with virtual nodes (Dynamo), range vs hash partitioning, tablet splitting and rebalancing (Bigtable), replica placement and anti-entropy (Merkle trees). Out: transaction semantics and indexing, which assume replication/partitioning are already solved and are covered next in Module 4. After this module Aman can name which replication and partitioning scheme a given system paper is using and derive its consistency and availability consequences before reading the consistency chapter.
topics: leader-based replication and lease-based mutation ordering (GFS's 60-second chunk lease)
quorum-based replication (read/write quorums, W+R>N)
consistent hashing with virtual nodes for partition placement
vector clocks for tracking concurrent writes to the same key
anti-entropy via Merkle trees for background replica repair
range partitioning vs hash partitioning trade-offs
dynamic tablet splitting and load-based rebalancing (Bigtable's ~100-200MB tablets)
atomic record append as a partitioning-aware write primitive
gossip-based membership and failure detection
disagreements: Strong, synchronously-replicated consistency vs. eventual consistency for large-scale storage

modules.title: Transactions, Indexes, and the Relational/NoSQL Split
modules.description: What a transaction actually guarantees at each isolation level, how an index turns a scan into a lookup, and why the relational and NoSQL camps made opposite bets on both.
modules.scope: In: ACID properties, isolation levels (read committed, snapshot isolation, serializable), two-phase commit, B-tree vs LSM-tree indexes and write amplification, the relational normalized model vs document/wide-column/key-value models. Out: distributed consensus underneath 2PC/Paxos-replicated transactions, covered next in Module 6. After this module Aman can read 'ACID' or 'BASE' on a product page and know exactly which guarantees are being claimed and which are being quietly dropped.
topics: ACID properties and what each one actually constrains
isolation levels: read committed, snapshot isolation, serializable, and the anomalies each still allows
two-phase commit as the classic distributed-transaction primitive
B-tree indexes vs LSM-tree indexes (SSTables, compaction, write amplification)
single-row atomic read-modify-write vs general cross-row transactions
the relational normalized model vs document/wide-column/key-value data models
why Dynamo-lineage stores deliberately do not offer general transactions
Spanner's externally-consistent transactions via TrueTime and 2PC over Paxos groups

modules.title: Consistency Models: Linearizability, CAP, and PACELC
modules.description: Why CAP is the wrong question and PACELC is the right one: what a system actually gives up during a partition, and what it gives up every single day when there isn't one.
modules.scope: In: linearizability, the CAP theorem's actual claim (and its limits), the PACELC framework (partition: availability vs consistency; else: latency vs consistency), external consistency via synchronized clocks (TrueTime). Out: the consensus protocols (Raft/Paxos/ZooKeeper) that implement a chosen consistency level, covered next in Module 6. After this module Aman can classify any storage system in this course as PA/EL, PC/EC, or PC/EL and predict its behavior both during and absent a partition.
topics: linearizability as the strongest single-object consistency guarantee
the CAP theorem's actual claim and why it under-specifies normal-operation behavior
PACELC: partition-mode (A vs C) and else-mode (L vs C) as two independent trade-offs
PA/EL systems (Dynamo): always-writeable, consistency sacrificed even absent partitions
PC/EC systems: full ACID databases paying both availability and latency costs
PC/EL systems (PNUTS-style): latency-for-consistency trade absent partitions, availability sacrificed during one
TrueTime and externally-consistent commit timestamps as Spanner's answer to the trade-off
why systems that trade consistency for availability during partitions tend to also trade it for latency normally
disagreements: Strong, synchronously-replicated consistency vs. eventual consistency for large-scale storage

modules.title: Consensus and Coordination: Paxos, Raft, Leases, and ZooKeeper/etcd
modules.description: How a set of unreliable machines agrees on one value -- a leader, a log entry, a lock -- and the coordination services (Chubby, ZooKeeper, etcd) built on top of that agreement.
modules.scope: In: the consensus problem, Raft's leader-election/log-replication/safety decomposition, majority-quorum commits, ZooKeeper's znodes/watches/Zab and its use as a coordination kernel, leases as a time-bounded consensus shortcut. Out: application-level use of these primitives for service discovery and dispatch, which appears later as a comparison point in Module 19 (Uber's Ringpop vs. ZooKeeper). After this module Aman can explain why a five-node Raft or Paxos cluster tolerates exactly two failures, and what a lease buys you that a lock doesn't.
topics: the consensus problem: agreement despite failures and asynchrony
Raft's three independent subproblems: leader election, log replication, safety
randomized election timeouts and why they prevent repeated split votes
majority-quorum commit: a minority of slow servers cannot slow the system down
Raft's joint-consensus membership-change mechanism
Paxos state machines under Bigtable's Chubby lock service and Spanner's spanservers
leases as a time-bounded alternative to indefinite locks (GFS chunk leases, Spanner leader leases)
ZooKeeper's znode hierarchy, ephemeral nodes, and one-shot watches as building blocks for locks and leader election
why ZooKeeper serves reads locally and unlinearized while keeping writes linearizable via Zab
disagreements: Is Raft's understandability advantage over Paxos decisive in practice?

modules.title: Distributed File and Object Storage: GFS, HDFS, S3, and Tectonic
modules.description: The blob-storage layer underneath every database and every training job: single-master metadata, large immutable chunks, and the lineage from GFS through HDFS to today's disaggregated object stores.
modules.scope: In: GFS's single-master architecture and 64MB chunking rationale, atomic record append, chunk replication and lease-based write ordering, HDFS as GFS's open-source descendant (architecture only, not re-derived), S3-style object storage's eventual-to-strong-consistency evolution, Tectonic as a modern disaggregated storage fabric. Out: the structured-storage layer built on top of files (Bigtable/tablets), covered in Modules 3-4. After this module Aman has the file/object-storage vocabulary needed for Part D's training-cluster storage module, which cites Tectonic directly.
topics: single-master metadata architecture and why clients never route file data through the master
64MB chunk size rationale and the <64-bytes-per-chunk in-memory metadata budget

object storage's shift from eventual to strong read-after-write consistency over the 2010s-2020s

Bigtable's SSTables as the structured layer riding on top of a GFS-style file layer

modules.title: Messaging and Streams: Logs, Queues, Exactly-Once, and Idempotency
modules.description: Why Kafka modeled a message broker as a dumb, stateless log instead of a smart, stateful queue, and how idempotency keys give you exactly-once behavior on top of an at-least-once network.
modules.scope: In: log-structured broker storage and segment files, pull vs push consumption, consumer-tracked offsets vs broker-tracked acknowledgment, page-cache-reliant IO and zero-copy transfer, exactly-once semantics, idempotency keys as the general retry-safety pattern. Out: batch/stream compute frameworks that consume these logs, covered next in Module 9. After this module Aman has the exactly-once/idempotency vocabulary that Module 18 (Stripe) and Module 23 (AI billing) both build directly on.

exactly-once semantics as an achieved property, not a network guarantee

modules.title: Batch and Stream Processing: The MapReduce to Spark/Flink Lineage
modules.description: The map/reduce contract that made cluster-scale batch computation tractable, and why Spark's lineage-based fault tolerance replaced replication-based recovery for iterative and interactive workloads.
modules.scope: In: MapReduce's map/reduce type contract and failure-recovery asymmetry (map re-executed, reduce output kept), input splitting, Spark RDDs and lineage-based fault tolerance, coarse-grained transformations as what makes cheap fault tolerance possible, in-memory persistence across queries. Out: the messaging layer that often feeds these pipelines (Module 8) and training-data-specific pipelines (Part D, Module 32), which cite this module rather than re-deriving it. After this module Aman can explain why Spark is 20x faster than Hadoop for iterative workloads without needing to open the Spark source.

modules.title: Services, APIs, and the Trust Boundary: Microservices, Service Mesh, Backpressure, Rate Limiting, and Zero Trust
modules.description: The architectural decisions that shape how independently-deployed services talk to each other safely and under load: service boundaries, mesh-level traffic control, backpressure, and zero-trust identity.
modules.scope: In: monolith-to-SOA migration trade-offs, service-IDL/RPC design, sidecar/service-mesh traffic shaping conceptually, backpressure mechanisms (bounded queues, load shedding), token-bucket and sliding-window rate limiting, zero-trust access (BeyondCorp), relationship-based authorization (Zanzibar). modules.title: Reliability Engineering: SLOs, Observability, and Resilience Patterns
modules.description: The vocabulary and mechanisms for stating what 'reliable' means (SLI/SLO/SLA), seeing whether you're meeting it (metrics/logs/traces), and surviving when a dependency stops cooperating (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads).

modules.title: YouTube and Vitess: Sharded MySQL at Video Scale, and What Isn't Public

modules.title: Netflix Video Infrastructure: Open Connect CDN and Per-Title Encoding
modules.description: How a single FreeBSD appliance was pushed from 40 Gbps to 100 Gbps of video, and how per-title encoding replaced one fixed bitrate ladder with one tuned to each video's own complexity.

modules.title: Netflix Resilience and Personalization: Chaos Engineering and the Offline/Nearline/Online Split

modules.title: WhatsApp, Twitter, and Instagram: Messaging and Feed Architectures at Scale

modules.title: Airbnb: Search Ranking, Payment Idempotency, and the Monolith-to-SOA Migration
modules.description: Airbnb's own published account of three engineering problems inside one two-sided marketplace: replacing a hand-tuned scoring function with a two-tower deep network, keeping a guest's payment from executing twice across a service-oriented architecture, and the monolith-to-SOA migration that let both evolve independently.

Out: re-deriving the general SOA cost/benefit analysis and Service IDL design rationale, which Module 10 already covers -- this module refers to it by number rather than repeating it, and instead uses the migration as the case study that let the search and payments teams in this module iterate independently.

the 2020 two-tower architecture, its reported online A/B-test deltas, and the O(N*H*(Q+L)) to O(N*Hl*L + Hq*Q) latency-complexity reduction

why an SOA turns a single logical payment operation into a distributed transaction, and Airbnb's write-repair alternative to two-phase commit
Orpheus: the three-phase (pre-RPC/RPC/post-RPC) idempotency library, its two ground rules, row-level lease locks, and request-level vs entity-level keys
the replica-lag double-payment failure mode and why idempotency state is read only from the sharded master database
Orpheus's five-nines (99.999%) payment-consistency result, its extension to Kafka event processing, and contrast with Stripe's Idempotency-Key header (Module 18)
the monolith-to-SOA migration's Service IDL and make-me-a-service scaffolding tool, recapped briefly with reference to Module 10's general treatment
the payments organization's specific four-phase SOA migration (Pricing, Payouts, Bookings, Data Migration) and its parallel-systems transformation layer
disagreements: Does deep learning retire feature engineering, or just relocate it into architecture design? (Airbnb's own launch optimism vs. its 2020 reintroduction of monotonicity/position structure)

parts.title: AI Inference Platform Design: Client to GPU
parts.description: The complete system between a client and a GPU backend -- gateway, identity, billing, routing, streaming, agents, caching, safety, data, tenancy -- given full treatment as the part Aman builds against most directly.

modules.title: Edge and API Gateway for AI Inference Platforms
modules.description: Why LLM inference traffic breaks generic HTTP load balancing, and the gateway architecture (auth check, rate limiter, router, provider call, async accounting) that OpenAI-, Anthropic-, and open-source-gateway-style platforms converge on instead.
modules.scope: In: the request lifecycle through a gateway (virtual-key auth -> rate limiter -> router -> provider call), why long-running, stateful, partially-cached inference sessions break path- or round-robin-based L7 balancing, the ext-proc extension pattern for reusing existing gateway infrastructure, async off-critical-path spend logging. Out: GPU-side routing signals and the backend interface itself, covered in Module 25; identity and rate-limit mechanics, covered next in Module 22. After this module Aman has the top-of-stack request lifecycle that every later Part C module attaches a piece to.
topics: the LiteLLM-style request lifecycle: virtual-key auth+budget check -> parallel rate limiter -> router -> provider call
why inference sessions are long-running, resource-intensive, and partially stateful (in-memory token caches) unlike typical web requests
why path-based or round-robin L7 balancing lacks model-identity and request-criticality awareness
the ext-proc extension pattern: reusing an existing Envoy/Gateway-API-capable gateway instead of building a bespoke one
async, off-critical-path spend logging and rate-limit accounting as background tasks
virtual keys carrying hard limits, soft limits with alerts, model whitelists, and per-key rate limits
why a global AI API's edge tier caches almost nothing, unlike a classical CDN's edge tier
spend rolling up from key to user to team as an organizational hierarchy

modules.title: Identity, Rate Limits, and Quotas: API Keys, Orgs, and Token-Bucket Enforcement
modules.description: The org/workspace/service-account identity hierarchy as OpenAI and Anthropic's own rate-limit documentation incidentally reveals it, and the two competing philosophies -- fixed-window multi-dimension counters vs. continuously-replenishing token buckets -- for enforcing limits on it.
modules.scope: In: usage-tier and workspace-budget structures, spend limits vs. rate limits as distinct mechanisms with different error signatures, token-bucket vs. fixed-window vs. sliding-window enforcement, per-dimension limits (RPM/RPD/TPM/TPD/IPM vs. RPM/ITPM/OTPM), workspace-level limits against an org-wide ceiling, zero-trust and relationship-based authorization applied to an API platform. Coverage note: auth-identity is thin -- no platform has published a dedicated API-key/OAuth architecture document; this module draws the identity hierarchy from what OpenAI's and Anthropic's rate-limit docs reveal incidentally, plus BeyondCorp/Zanzibar for the underlying zero-trust and authorization mechanisms, and states this gap explicitly.
topics: usage tiers keyed to cumulative spend (OpenAI) vs. named plan tiers with explicit monthly spend caps (Anthropic)
spend limits vs. rate limits: two mechanisms, two different error signatures (no retry-after vs. always retry-after)
token-bucket enforcement: capacity continuously replenished rather than reset at fixed intervals
fixed-window vs. sliding-window rate limiting and the up-to-2x burst a fixed window allows at a boundary
per-dimension limit sets: OpenAI's six independent dimensions vs. Anthropic's three
workspace-level limits set below the org-wide limit, with unused allocation available to other workspaces
why 429s from unsuccessful requests still count against the limit, and what that implies for retry design
BeyondCorp-style zero trust and Zanzibar-style relationship-based authorization applied to org/team/resource permissions on an API platform
disagreements: Fixed-window vs. sliding-window rate limiting
How should token-based LLM rate limits be enforced when true cost is only known after generation?

modules.title: Billing and Metering: Ledger Design, Idempotency, Holds, and Reconciliation
modules.description: How Stripe's idempotency-key and real-time-metering patterns get reused, nearly unchanged, to deduct token-based credits exactly once, hold funds against a still-streaming response, and reconcile a running ledger against a periodic invoice.
modules.scope: In: credit-deduction ledger design reusing the idempotency-key three-state model, holds/pre-authorization for long-running streams whose final cost is unknown at request start, reconciliation between real-time metering and invoicing, abuse/fraud control touchpoints. Out: the rate-limit enforcement layer that runs before billing even begins, covered in Module 22, and the Stripe patterns this module is built on, covered in Module 18. After this module Aman can design a credit ledger that survives a retried, a cancelled, and a partially-streamed request without double-charging or losing revenue.
topics: credit-deduction as an idempotent operation keyed the same way Stripe keys a payment retry
the three-state (absent/in-flight/complete) model applied to a still-streaming token count
holds/pre-authorization: reserving a worst-case credit amount before a long stream's true cost is known
reconciliation: releasing the unused portion of a hold once the actual token count is final
real-time continuous-balance metering (Metronome-style) vs. legacy async meter-event aggregation, and why high-event-volume LLM usage needs the former
invoicing at the org/workspace rollup level, consistent with Module 22's spend hierarchy
abuse/fraud control touchpoints: anomalous usage-rate detection, stolen-key patterns, chargeback-equivalent handling
why a mid-stream cancellation (Module 26) must resolve to a correct partial charge, not a full hold release or a full charge

modules.title: Request Routing, Admission Control, and SLO Tiers: Fallbacks and Graceful Degradation
modules.description: How a platform decides which request gets served now, which waits, which gets a smaller model instead, and which gets rejected outright -- the layer where an incident actually gets fought, even though no source in this map documents 'incident response' as its own topic.
modules.scope: In: routing dimensions (model, region, tier/priority, version pinning), quota-checked-at-admission vs. checked-at-scheduling-time, queueing and backpressure at the gateway, batch vs. interactive lane separation, SLO-tiered service classes, fallback and graceful-degradation design (model downgrade, region failover), KV-cache-utilization/queue-depth as inference-aware routing signals. Coverage note: incident-patterns has no dedicated source in this map at all; this module folds the closest available material -- graceful degradation and admission control -- into itself rather than scheduling a standalone module on an uncovered subtopic.
topics: routing dimensions: model, region, tier/priority, explicit version pinning
Borg's quota-checked-at-admission precedent: reject immediately on insufficient quota rather than waiting for scheduling
queueing disciplines and backpressure propagating from the gateway back to the client
batch vs. interactive lane separation as a scheduling-class decision, not just a priority number
SLO-tiered service classes and what differs across tiers (latency budget, queueing position, fallback eligibility)
fallback design: model downgrade, region failover, and what must be true for a fallback to be safe (idempotency, compatible output contract)
KV-cache utilization and queue depth as the model-server-aware routing signals a generic L7 balancer lacks
why 'incident response' for an inference platform is mostly these same mechanisms exercised under stress, not a separate system

modules.title: The GPU Backend Handoff: Designing the Interface to Multi-Node Serving
modules.description: The contract at the boundary between the platform layer this course has built so far and the multi-node GPU serving stack Aman already knows in depth -- designed here as an interface, not re-derived as a mechanism.
modules.scope: In: the signals a stateful multi-node GPU backend must expose across this boundary (KV-cache utilization, queue depth), why generic health checks are insufficient for this backend, model/version pinning across the interface, backpressure propagation from GPU backend to gateway. Out: everything about how the GPU backend itself works internally -- interconnects, PD disaggregation, wide EP, Dynamo/llm-d/vLLM/SGLang internals -- which is the multi-node-llm-inference course's subject and is referenced, not repeated. Coverage note: gpu-backend-handoff is a thin subtopic; this module is scoped narrowly to what the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension's own routing-signal design actually documents, stated as a first-principles interface design rather than a surveyed one.
topics: why a stateful, partially-cached GPU backend cannot be treated as an interchangeable pool behind a generic health check
KV-cache utilization as an exposed backend signal the platform layer routes on
queue depth as a second exposed signal, distinct from and complementary to KV-cache utilization
model identity and version pinning propagated across the platform-to-backend boundary
backpressure propagating from a saturated GPU backend up through the platform layer to the client
the explicit non-goal: this module designs the contract, not the GPU-side mechanism the multi-node-llm-inference course already covers
what a stable interface must guarantee across a backend upgrade (e.g. a new PD-disaggregation topology) without the platform layer changing

modules.title: Streaming, Cancellation, and Resumption: SSE, WebSockets, and Long-Running Requests
modules.description: The typed SSE event lifecycle a modern LLM API streams over, why streaming makes moderation structurally harder, and the sequence-number-based protocol for resuming a stream after a client disconnects.
modules.scope: In: SSE event taxonomy (created/in_progress/delta/completed/failed) and per-item tool-call/code-interpreter sub-events, why partial completions are harder to moderate than whole ones and why moderation scores only arrive after full output, background-mode resumption via sequence-number cursors, cancellation semantics. Out: the billing resolution of a cancelled or disconnected stream, covered in Module 23. After this module Aman can design a resumable streaming protocol and state precisely what it cannot guarantee about safety review of partial output.
topics: SSE typed lifecycle events: created, in_progress, output_text.delta, completed, failed
per-item streaming sub-events for function/tool calls and code-interpreter output
why streaming structurally weakens moderation: partial completions are harder to evaluate and full-output moderation scores arrive too late to gate a delta
background mode: a response created with background+stream flags, resumable via a tracked sequence_number cursor
resumption's precondition: only possible if the original response was created with stream=true
temporary server-side storage windows for resumable response data
cancellation semantics and what a client can and cannot assume about work already done server-side
contrast with a structurally different low-latency streaming protocol stack (Twitch's live video) to sharpen what is specific to token streaming

modules.title: Tool Use, Agent Harnesses, and Sandboxes for Code Execution
modules.description: The general design problem of an agent harness and the sandbox layer beneath it -- isolation-mechanism choice, snapshot/restore warm pools, egress and secrets policy, per-tenant limits, and execution-time billing -- checked against Anthropic, OpenAI/Codex, E2B, and Modal's own specs as evidence, not as the spine.
modules.scope: In: isolation-mechanism trade-offs for a code-execution sandbox (shared-kernel containers, hardware-virtualized microVMs, gVisor's user-space kernel, WebAssembly's compile-time software fault isolation, OS-level sandboxing for local/single-tenant execution), snapshot/restore and warm pools as the startup-latency-vs-isolation trade-off, egress policy and secrets handling, per-tenant resource limits and host-level scheduling/density, session/thread state and identity, streamed events and turn-level approval pauses distinguished from Module 26's connection-level resumption, tool discovery/validation, and execution-time billing as a cost model. Vendor specifics (exact RAM/disk figures, exact pricing tiers) appear in comparison tables as evidence for the design space, not as the module's spine. Out: the RL-training use of sandboxes as verifiers/environments, covered in Module 37, which this module is a direct prerequisite for.
topics: isolation mechanisms compared: shared-kernel containers, Firecracker-style hardware-virtualized microVMs, gVisor's user-space kernel (Sentry/Gofer), WebAssembly's compile-time software fault isolation, OS-level sandboxing (Seatbelt/Landlock+seccomp) for local execution

startup latency, isolation strength, and host density as the trade-off axis distinguishing the five mechanisms, with Firecracker's measured overhead/boot-time/density numbers as the evidentiary anchor
snapshot/restore and warm pools: checkpoint-then-restore-window designs (Anthropic, E2B, Modal, OpenAI) as answers to the same startup-latency problem
egress policy defaults (default-deny vs. default-allow) and secrets handling, including OpenAI Codex Cloud's two-phase setup/agent network split with pre-agent-phase secret purge

per-tenant resource limits and host-level scheduling/density, including a worked derivation of microVM overhead-as-percentage-of-entitlement and its connection to Borg's quota-checked-at-admission pattern
session/thread state: sandbox identity as a session handle, and the harness-level thread/turn/item lifecycle (create/resume/fork/archive)
streamed events and turn-level approval pauses (Anthropic's pause_turn, Codex's approval request), explicitly distinguished from Module 26's connection-level stream resumption
tool discovery and validation: fixed auto-provisioned sub-tools vs. an open MCP/skills surface, and the multicomputer-environment confusion risk when client-provided and sandboxed tools coexist
execution-time billing as a cost model: minimum billing increments, free-allowance pools, per-hour/per-session rates, and a worked $/hour comparison across vendors
disagreements: Which isolation mechanism should be the default for a multi-tenant code-execution sandbox: hardware-virtualized microVMs (E2B/Firecracker), a user-space kernel with a full-VM escape hatch (Modal/gVisor), or OS-level sandboxing for the single-tenant local case (OpenAI Codex CLI)?

modules.title: Platform Prompt/Prefix Caching: Tiers, TTLs, and Billing Implications
modules.description: Two opposite cache-lookup philosophies -- Anthropic's explicit breakpoints vs. OpenAI's automatic longest-prefix match -- and the arithmetic of when a 1.25x-to-2x write premium and a 0.1x read discount actually pay for themselves.
modules.scope: In: explicit-breakpoint vs. automatic-prefix-match cache lookup, pricing multipliers for writes and reads, TTL mechanics and the response-generation-time-counts-against-lifetime trap, concurrent-request cold-cache-miss behavior, minimum cacheable prompt length, whether cached tokens count against a rate limit. Out: the general caching-invalidation mechanism from Module 2, which this module treats as background and specializes into a billing-bearing mechanism unique to LLM platforms.
topics: explicit cache breakpoints (up to 4 per request, ordered tools->system->messages) vs. automatic longest-to-shortest prefix lookup
pricing multipliers: 5-minute write at 1.25x, 1-hour write at 2x, read at 0.1x (or lower) of base input price
default cache lifetime and the trap that response-generation time counts against it, not just idle time
concurrent-request cold-cache-miss behavior: a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins
minimum cacheable prompt length thresholds and silent no-op behavior below them
breakpoint-level invalidation cascade: a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it
the fork on whether cached tokens count toward a throughput rate limit, and its effect on a heavy-cache-reuse workload's effective throughput ceiling
manual cache-clearing availability (or its absence) as an operational lever
disagreements: Should cached tokens count against a customer's rate limit?

modules.title: Safety and Moderation Pipelines: Pre/Post Filters, Classifiers, and Policy Routing
modules.description: A 13-category classifier scoring endpoint meant as a policy signal, not an automatic gate, set against a four-stage pipeline that treats safety as continuous from policy design through training to real-time enforcement.
modules.scope: In: the moderation-endpoint classifier taxonomy and confidence-score output shape, the 'signal not automatic block' design philosophy, the alternative four-stage pipeline (policy -> training integration -> pre-deployment evaluation -> real-time enforcement), CBRN/cyber as a distinct high-risk evaluation category, policy routing as a pattern. Out: the privacy-preserving aggregate-analysis pipeline (Clio), covered as a data-governance mechanism in Module 30 rather than a safety-classifier mechanism here.
topics: the 13-category moderation taxonomy and its per-category boolean-flag plus confidence-score (0-1) output shape
'treat as policy signal, not automatic block' as an explicit design recommendation, with review-before-action as its corollary
the four-stage alternative: policy development, training-time behavior shaping, pre-deployment safety/risk/bias evaluation, real-time classifier enforcement
classifiers as prompted or specially fine-tuned models detecting policy violations in real time
CBRN and cyber-harm as a distinct pre-deployment risk-assessment category from general safety evaluation
policy routing: directing a request to a different model or behavior based on a classifier's output
why streaming (Module 26) structurally weakens any post-generation moderation gate

Policy-routing decision: a classifier score branching a request to a restricted model, a refusal, or normal generation
CBRN/cyber risk assessment positioned as a distinct gate alongside, not inside, general safety evaluation
disagreements: Should safety moderation be a pre-generation blocking gate or a post-generation signal?

modules.title: Data and Observability: Conversation Storage, Retention, Privacy, and Per-Token Tracing
modules.description: Clio's four-stage privacy-preserving pipeline for learning from a million real conversations without a human ever reading one, and the per-token metrics and cross-system tracing that make an LLM platform's own behavior legible.
modules.scope: In: conversation/log storage and retention windows, Clio's facet-extraction/clustering/private-info-excluded-description/hierarchy pipeline with its minimum-cluster-size floor, consent boundaries for using conversation data in training, per-token metrics as the LLM-specific observability primitive, cross-system tracing from gateway through scheduler to GPU, cost attribution. Clio's four-stage pipeline: facet extraction, semantic clustering, private-info-excluded cluster description, hierarchy building

a model verifying its own cluster summaries are non-identifying before a human analyst ever sees them
correlation between an automated analysis system and a separate trust-and-safety classification system as a validation technique
consent boundaries for using stored conversation data in future model training
per-token metrics (time-to-first-token, inter-token latency, tokens/sec) as the LLM-specific observability primitive beyond generic request latency

cost attribution per request/tenant as the economic close of the observability loop

Retention-and-consent boundary diagram: what is stored, for how long, and under which consent condition it may feed training
Per-token metrics timeline for one streamed response: time-to-first-token, inter-token latency, total tokens/sec
Cross-system trace: one request's span across gateway, router/scheduler, and GPU backend, cost attributed at each hop

modules.title: Multi-Tenancy, Isolation, and Capacity/Cost Management
modules.description: The live fork between running dedicated GPU clusters per customer to kill noisy-neighbor variance and running one shared pool behind per-key budgets to maximize utilization -- and the capacity-planning arithmetic that decides between them.
modules.scope: In: dedicated-per-tenant-cluster isolation vs. shared-pool-plus-virtual-key isolation, the utilization-vs-isolation trade-off, Borg's quota-checked-at-admission precedent applied to tenant isolation, capacity planning for bursty or idle tenant traffic, cost attribution feeding back into capacity decisions. Coverage note: the primary source for the dedicated-cluster model is a third-party-relayed, unverified claim about one vendor -- flagged explicitly rather than presented as confirmed fact.

cost attribution (Module 30) as the feedback signal that should, in principle, drive capacity re-provisioning
why this module states the dedicated-cluster figures as unverified third-party claims rather than confirmed vendor disclosure

Borg-style admission-by-quota adapted to tenant-level isolation rather than job-level admission
Source-confidence flag on the Fireworks figures: third-party-relayed claim, not vendor-confirmed, marked explicitly on the diagram
disagreements: Dedicated per-tenant GPU pools vs. shared pooled GPUs with per-key limits for inference multi-tenancy

parts.title: AI Training Infrastructure: Systems Level
parts.description: Pre-training, post-training, and RL infrastructure as systems -- data, storage, scheduling, fault tolerance, and framework architecture -- with distributed-training internals deliberately excluded.

modules.title: Training Data Pipelines: Crawl/Ingest, Filtering/Dedup, Tokenization, and Sharded Datasets
modules.description: The URL-level, document-level, and line-level deduplication cascade Meta disclosed for Llama 3's pre-training corpus, read as an application of the batch-processing lineage from Part A rather than a new mechanism.
modules.scope: In: URL-level and document-level (global MinHash) deduplication, aggressive line-level (ccNet-style) deduplication removing lines repeated across a document bucket, fasttext/RoBERTa quality classifiers, a 176-language fasttext language-ID model, why the underlying compute substrate is the MapReduce/Spark lineage already covered. Out: experiment-tracking and evaluation-pipeline tooling for pre-training data -- not a subtopic with any source coverage in this map, and not scheduled as its own module; noted here as an explicit gap rather than invented content. modules.title: Storage and Checkpointing at Scale: Cluster Network Topology
modules.description: Tectonic's 240PB storage fabric and the three-layer Clos network that connects 24,000 H100s into training pods, with checkpoint writes as the bursty workload that has to survive both.
modules.scope: In: Tectonic's 240PB/2TB/s-sustained/7TB/s-peak storage fabric, per-GPU checkpoint state size (1MB-4GB) and bursty-write saturation, the three-layer Clos network topology (rack -> pod -> cluster, 1:7 oversubscription), why this is GFS's chunked-replication idea applied at a different point in the training stack. modules.title: Cluster Scheduling and Orchestration: Slurm, the Borg/Kubernetes Lineage, Ray, and MAST
modules.description: Four different answers to 'who decides what runs where': Slurm's centralized heartbeat model, Borg's priority-and-quota admission control, Ray's actor/task/object-store primitives, and Meta's MAST -- named but not detailed beyond what Meta has disclosed.

modules.title: Fault Tolerance and Elasticity: Checkpoint/Restart, Stragglers, Node Health, and Incident Patterns
modules.description: 466 job interruptions in 54 days of Llama 3 pre-training, three-quarters of them hardware-attributed, and the heartbeat-and-checkpoint machinery that still got the cluster to over 90% effective training time.
modules.scope: In: the 466-interruption/54-day taxonomy (47 planned, 419 unexpected, 78% hardware-attributed, faulty-GPU at 30.1% and HBM3 failure at 17.2%), the >90%-effective-training-time result despite this failure rate, MegaScale's heartbeat-based real-time anomaly detection and 3D-visualization straggler diagnosis, checkpoint/restart as the universal recovery primitive. modules.title: Post-Training Pipelines: SFT/Preference Data Flows, Evaluation Gates, and Model Registries
modules.description: Llama 3's six rounds of SFT, reward modeling, rejection sampling, and DPO, with PagedAttention's 2x rejection-sampling speedup as the one place inference-serving machinery visibly leaks into a training pipeline.
modules.scope: In: the 6-round SFT->reward-modeling->rejection-sampling->DPO pipeline, PagedAttention's throughput contribution specifically to rejection sampling, evaluation gates between rounds as Llama 3's paper documents them, the RLHF dataflow modeled as a DAG of NN computations with many-to-many resharding edges as the systems-level abstraction. Out: model-registry and general experiment-tracking tooling beyond what Llama 3's release framing documents -- a genuine gap, stated explicitly rather than filled with generic MLOps assumptions.

PagedAttention adopted specifically for rejection sampling, yielding over 2x throughput there -- an inference-serving technique inside a training pipeline
evaluation gates between rounds as Llama 3's paper documents the process, without generalizing beyond that one disclosed pipeline

modules.title: RL Training Infrastructure: Environments as Services, Rollout Generation, and Trainer/Rollout Decoupling
modules.description: Why RL post-training is an inference workload wearing a training hat, and the three competing philosophies -- hard version-rejection, depth-bounded queues, importance-sampling correction -- for how stale a rollout is allowed to be before it can't be trusted.
modules.scope: In: environments-as-services framing (state/action/reward loop packaged as a reusable service, with sandboxes plugged in as verifiers), rollout generation's direct coupling to inference-serving mechanics, trainer/rollout decoupling architectures, the staleness-management taxonomy, the concrete arithmetic of why generation dominates RL wall-clock time. Out: the specific framework implementations comparing this decoupling in practice, covered next in Module 38.
topics: environments as a packaged state/action/reward loop, letting task-specific work (datasets, tools, reward functions) reuse shared eval/RL infrastructure
sandboxes (Module 27) plugging directly into environments as verifiers for secure code execution
rollout generation as fundamentally an inference-serving workload: continuous batching, paged KV cache, and the multi-node-llm-inference course's mechanics all apply here unmodified
the dominant architecture: an inference pool (vLLM/SGLang, continuous) and a training pool (optimizer, continuous) connected by a weight-synchronization protocol
staleness management, category one: hard version-rejection of samples too far behind the current policy
staleness management, category two: depth-bounded queues capping how many stale samples can accumulate between generation and training
staleness management, category three: importance-sampling correction, typically clipped, reweighting stale samples that do get used
the concrete arithmetic: a 32B model generating 32K tokens/rollout across 512 sequences at ~1.2K tok/s takes ~3.7 hours on one H100, which is why this is the bottleneck
weight-sync latency spread from ~500ms (standard NCCL broadcast) to ~20ms (bucketed) to ~1-10ms (per-forward-pass swap, one outlier framework)

modules.title: Comparing the Open-Source RL Frameworks: verl, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, AReaL, slime, and NeMo-RL
modules.description: Six frameworks' answers to the same trainer/rollout-decoupling question, from verl's hybrid single-/multi-controller resharding to AReaL's fully asynchronous microservices, read against a 16-framework survey that found no consensus.
modules.scope: In: verl's hybrid single-controller/multi-controller design and 3D-HybridEngine resharding, OpenRLHF's Ray-based Actor/Reward/Reference/Critic separation, SkyRL's modularity emphasis, AReaL's fully asynchronous microservice architecture and staleness knob, slime's SGLang-native training/rollout/buffer split (GLM's production framework), NeMo-RL's dual DTensor/Megatron backend design, and the Ray-orchestrated-vs-native-async orchestration fork across the wider 16-framework ecosystem. Out: re-deriving the staleness-management taxonomy itself, established in Module 37, which this module applies to six concrete systems.

parts.title: Frontier and Synthesis
parts.description: What remains genuinely unsettled across classical systems, AI inference platforms, and AI training infrastructure, as of this course's as-of date.

modules.title: Where the Field Still Disagrees and What Is Changing: Consistency, Multi-Tenancy, Async RL, and the Next Edition
modules.description: A synthesis, not a survey: the disagreements this course could not resolve because the field has not resolved them, revisited together, plus what is actively moving as of this course's as-of date.
modules.scope: In: a recap of the strong-vs-eventual-consistency fork now over a decade old and still unresolved as a general question even as specific systems have picked sides; the dedicated-vs-shared multi-tenancy-isolation fork, likely to be settled by cost economics rather than an architecture paper; the async-RL trainer/rollout fork and the 16-framework ecosystem's continued lack of convergence; the rate-limit-enforcement-philosophy fork as a live product decision. Out: introducing any new disagreement not already raised in an earlier module -- this module recaps, per the course guide's requirement that a course end at the frontier rather than open a new one. Explicitly time-stamped throughout, including DDIA's February 2026 second edition as a marker that even the foundational textbook is still being re-synthesized.
topics: recap: strong synchronous replication (Spanner) vs. always-writeable eventual consistency (Dynamo), fifteen-plus years on, still a live architectural choice rather than a resolved question
recap: dedicated-per-tenant GPU clusters vs. shared pools with per-key budgets, and why this is likely to be settled by cost economics rather than a definitive architecture paper
recap: synchronous vs. asynchronous trainer/rollout coupling, and why a 16-framework survey found three orthogonal staleness philosophies rather than one converged answer
recap: pessimistic-estimate-and-adjust vs. optimistic-admit-and-reconcile rate-limit enforcement as two live philosophies, not a settled one
